title: Catastrophizing: Why Your Brain Jumps to the Worst-Case Scenario (and How to Stop)
summary: Catastrophizing is a cognitive distortion that fuels anxiety and depression. Learn what causes catastrophic thinking, who it affects, and evidence-based ways to stop it.
body_markdown:
## Causes of Catastrophizing


At its core, catastrophizing tends to come from two places: fear and a quiet belief that one cannot handle whatever bad thing might happen. The thought is rarely about the situation itself. It is about the assumption that the person will be helpless when it arrives. That assumption usually has a history and several recognizable factors contribute to it.


- **Childhood environment.** A person who grew up with a parent who panicked easily, overreacted to small problems, or treated every mistake as a disaster tends to learn the same thinking style. Children raised by perfectionists or harshly critical caregivers also learn early that things can go wrong fast and that they will be blamed when they do.
- **Early exposure to real worst-case events.** Some people grew up watching genuine catastrophes happen: a parent losing a job, a sudden move, a family member relapsing, and concluded that the world is unpredictable and unsafe. Research summarized by the[National Institute of Mental Health](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/generalized-anxiety-disorder-gad) connects stressful environments and traumatic experiences to a higher risk of generalized anxiety disorder.
- **A hidden need for control.** Imagining the worst can feel like protection. If a person has already pictured the bad outcome, they will not be blindsided by it. Some people unconsciously create small versions of the feared outcome to get ahead of it, like starting an argument with a partner because they fear being left, so that at least the rejection happens on their terms. It is a painful kind of protection, but the brain treats it as protection all the same.
- **Co-occurring anxiety or depression.** Catastrophizing both feeds and is fed by other mental health conditions. A[2021 study of nurses in eastern China during the COVID-19 outbreak](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8013387/) found that more frequent use of catastrophizing as a coping strategy was associated with more anxiety or depressive symptoms.
- **Chronic pain and fatigue.** When the body is already under strain, the mind has less room to think flexibly. A randomized controlled trial in fibromyalgia patients, published in[Arthritis Research & Therapy](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3308108/) , found that pain catastrophizing scores were notably elevated in the patient sample, and that cognitive behavioral therapy was more effective than pharmacological treatment at bringing them down.
- **Sudden life changes.** Even calm, generally optimistic people can fall into what-if thinking when life shifts without warning. A serious diagnosis, a[job loss](https://lifestance.com/blog/how-to-cope-with-layoff-anxiety/) , a divorce, or a major change in routine can pull anyone into worst-case scenario thinking.


Each of these factors can produce catastrophic thoughts on its own, but they often stack. A person with a critical childhood environment, an underlying anxiety disorder, and a sudden life change will feel the pull of catastrophizing more sharply than someone with only one factor in play. The pattern becomes a clinical concern when it stops being situational and turns into the default way the mind responds to uncertainty, showing up in everyday decisions and getting in the way of sleep, work, or relationships.
